overlap.title: Behemoth and leviathan — what creatures does the Lord point Job to?
overlap.summary: The Lord’s speech from the whirlwind (40:6) sets two creatures before Job, behemoth and leviathan, and describes each at length. The KJV keeps both words as names. The verses quoted do not say what kind of creature either one is.
overlap.reasoning: The speech uses the two creatures to answer Job, so what they are bears on what the answer is. The description joins things said of a grazing animal and a creature of the water (grass, a river, a hook) with things that go beyond that (a flame from the mouth, heads in the plural in the psalm, a kingship over “all the children of pride”). If they are animals Job could see, the speech can be read as pointing to God’s rule over the made world; if they are creatures of another kind, it can be read as pointing to powers beyond ordinary animals. The text names them and does not say which.
overlap.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Possible readings: that they are two known animals described in heightened language; that they are animals no longer known; and that they are creatures of a kind other than ordinary animals, as Isaiah 27:1 speaks of leviathan beside “the dragon that is in the sea”. Each is an interpretation; the verses quoted state none of them, in the KJV or in the Hebrew quoted, and this record asserts none. The speech is in verse, and this record does not test its pictures against natural history. A shared name in the Psalms and Isaiah does not settle that the same creature is meant in Job. Two separate records compare the Greek, which has “beasts” at 40:15 and a common noun for a dragon or serpent at KJV 41:1; the Greek verses quoted in those records keep neither name. Check made for an answer elsewhere: the packaged KJV was searched for the words “behemoth” (Job 40:15 only) and “leviathan” (Job 41:1, Psalms 74:14, Psalms 104:26, Isaiah 27:1), and those verses were read. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible, and Job 40:15–41:34 was not compared with the Hebrew or the Greek verse by verse. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry.
